transcript.content: Hello, I am Dr. Smith. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. I'm here because I've been feeling extremely down, sad, and just completely depressed for the past seven months. It feels like I can't shake this heavy, gloomy mood no matter what I do.
Have you felt this low mood consistently every single day for the past seven months, or have there been periods of a few weeks where you felt completely back to your normal self?
Yes, it's been like this nearly every single day for the past seven months. I haven't had any moments where I felt back to my normal, healthy self—it's just been a constant, heavy cloud.
During these past seven months, have you lost interest or pleasure in almost all of the activities you used to enjoy?
I'm not really sure about that, to be honest. I haven't really noticed a loss of interest in my usual activities.

Since you haven't lost interest in your activities, have you been experiencing other physical symptoms like significant changes in your appetite, sleep patterns, or feeling physically slowed down or restless?

Yes, during this depression my appetite has dropped significantly and I've lost a lot of weight. But when my energy is high, I feel extremely restless and unable to sit still, like I'm constantly driven to move. I'm not really sure about any specific changes in my sleep patterns, though.

During those times when your energy is high and you feel restless, have you also found that you need much less sleep than usual, or that your thoughts are racing and you are talking much faster than normal?

Yes, during those high-energy times, my thoughts spin uncontrollably and jump from one idea to another, and I talk so fast and constantly that others find it hard to interrupt me. As for my sleep, I'm not really sure and haven't paid close attention to how much sleep I've been getting during those periods.
During those high-energy periods, have these symptoms been severe enough to cause significant problems at work or in your social life, or perhaps required a hospital stay?
I'm not quite sure about that, honestly. I haven't really thought about whether it caused major disruptions in my life, and I've never been hospitalized for it.

When you are in these high-energy states, do you find that you are still able to function at work or in your daily routine, or do these episodes clearly stand out as a noticeable change in your functioning to those around you?

Yes, people close to me definitely notice a drastic change when I'm in those states. They often point out how incredibly fast I'm talking and how I constantly jump from one project to another. My family has also been really concerned about how impulsively I start spending money during those times.

During these episodes of impulsive spending and racing thoughts, do you still manage to maintain your job responsibilities, or does your behavior cause you to miss work or get into trouble at your workplace?
I'm not really sure about how it affects my job, to be honest. I haven't really thought about whether it has caused direct trouble at work or made me miss days.

Can you recall the longest period these high-energy episodes have lasted, and do you feel that you could have continued working normally if you had chosen to, or was it truly impossible to maintain your usual work performance?

These high-energy periods typically last for about two weeks. During those times, far from being unable to work, I actually feel overflowing with energy and end up doing far more work than usual. I often find myself starting multiple projects and activities simultaneously because of how energized I am.
Besides never being hospitalized, have you ever experienced these high-energy episodes that lasted for an entire week or longer, or were they always shorter than that?
Yes, they definitely last for a week or longer. In fact, these high-energy periods usually go on for about two weeks.

latest_inference.note: The patient reports periods of elevated energy, racing thoughts, and impulsive behavior lasting two weeks, which meets the duration criteria for a manic or hypomanic episode. Because the patient reports being able to perform more work than usual during these periods (rather than experiencing severe impairment or requiring hospitalization), Bipolar II remains a strong candidate, but Bipolar I cannot be ruled out until we clarify if these periods reach the threshold of 'marked impairment' in other social or occupational domains.
